title: Spot the cluster
caption: The galaxy cluster PLCKESZ G286.6-31.3 behind the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope
celestial: PLCKESZ G286.6-31.3 · constellation Mensa · about z=0.21 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A starry field fills this picture, and the galaxy cluster PLCKESZ G286.6-31.3 hides among the stars. It is hard to pick out at first but shows up as a faint grouping of yellowish galaxies close to the middle of the frame. At lower left sits IC 2140, a globular star cluster.
The cluster contains up to 1000 galaxies, along with large amounts of hot gas and dark matter. Altogether its mass comes to 530 trillion times that of the Sun.

From Earth we see the cluster through the outer edges of the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's satellite galaxies. That is why the field is so crowded. Most of the objects in the frame are stars and star clusters inside the Large Magellanic Cloud, home to over 700 star clusters as well as giant and supergiant stars numbering in the hundreds of thousands.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope observed this field in visible and near-infrared light through V, R and I filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the cluster's galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

explore: The picture comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope, which has worked at ESO's La Silla Observatory since 1984 and has been used in research into gamma-ray bursts. The 67-million-pixel camera has been photographing faint, distant objects since 1999. The data were chosen from the ESO archive for the Hidden Treasures competition.
alt: A crowded star field with a faint group of yellowish galaxies near the center and a globular star cluster at lower left.
